extracted.intended_audience: independent inventors / pro se applicants (inventors and patent applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what constitutes prior art and how it is used to determine novelty (anticipation) and non-obviousness under the AIA and pre‑AIA, including statutory provisions, exceptions (grace period, common ownership), dates, and examiner burdens. Intended to help inventors understand examiner rejections and prepare/respond accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art constitutes those references or documents which may be used to determine novelty and/or non-obviousness of claimed subject matter in a patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes anything that can be used as examiner evidence (prior publications, patents, admissions of prior art, on-sale items, etc.). Prior art is the evidentiary basis for establishing a prima facie case of non‑patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common Types of Prior Art — Printed Documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed documents such as patents and published patent applications (domestic and foreign) and non‑patent literature (magazine articles, newspapers, electronic publications, on‑line databases, websites, Internet publications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP 2126–2128. Electronic or online materials may qualify as printed publications depending on dissemination and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant’s Admissions of Prior Art (AAPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made by applicant that certain information was 'prior art' (may appear in the background, drawings, or applicant remarks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissions by an applicant can be used as prior art against claims. See MPEP 2129. Beware of language in your specification that concedes prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Use or On Sale as Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use or sale (including offers to sell) can qualify as prior art if it occurred early enough to have an effective prior art date before the claimed invention's effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A document lacking an intrinsic prior art date may nonetheless provide evidence of public use or sale. Timing and proof of public availability/sale are critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Otherwise Available to the Public' (AIA 102(a)(1) catch‑all)
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA introduced 'otherwise available to the public' as a prior art category with examples such as oral presentations, demonstrations at trade shows, lectures/speeches, radio statements, YouTube videos, websites, or other online material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision captures non‑traditional disclosures that make subject matter publicly accessible. Some such disclosures may also qualify as printed publications under other provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of Patentability and Examiner's Prima Facie Burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimed inventions are presumed patentable until the examiner establishes a prima facie case that a patentability requirement is not met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prima facie case requires sufficient initial evidence (typically prior art) to support non‑patentability. The examiner's evidence often consists of prior publications, patents, admissions, on‑sale items, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (Novelty) — Single Reference Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation occurs when a single prior art reference describes, either expressly or inherently, each and every limitation of a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim requires limitations A, B, C, and D, a single reference that discloses A, B, C, and D anticipates. Inherent disclosure counts. Examiner must show every claim element is present in the single reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(1) — Novelty Statutory Text
rubrics_metrics.description: A person shall be entitled to a patent unless the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory basis for anticipation prior art under AIA for disclosures predating the effective filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(2) — Prior Art from Patents/Applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention was described in a patent issued under section 151, or in an application for patent published or deemed published under section 122(b), naming another inventor and effectively filed before the claimed invention's effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This addresses prior art that arises from earlier‑filed patent documents (including certain PCT/WIPO publications designating the U.S.). Requirements for 'effectively filed' dates are governed by 102(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA 102(b)(1) — One‑Year Grace Period Exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures made 1 year or less before the effective filing date shall not be prior art under 102(a)(1) if (A) the disclosure was made by the inventor (or someone who obtained it from the inventor), or (B) the subject matter had been publicly disclosed by the inventor before such disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a limited one‑year grace period for disclosures by the inventor or derived from the inventor. Properly document dates and authorship of early disclosures to rely on this exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Dates Relative to Grace Period (102(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: No exception applies to 102(a)(1) prior art disclosed before the claimed invention's grace period began; an AIA applicant's one‑year grace period can be based on the applicant's foreign priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosures earlier than the grace period cannot be excused. Foreign priority claims can affect the start of the one‑year window—ensure priority claims are perfected if relying on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102(a)(2) — Only U.S. Patent Documents Can Be 'Effectively Filed' Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Only a U.S. patent document can have a 102(a)(2) 'effectively filed' prior art date. The three types: U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications (PGPubs), and WIPO publications of PCT applications that designate the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non‑U.S. patent documents are not §102(a)(2) references unless they are part of a qualifying WIPO/PCT publication. No English requirement for WIPO publication; PCT date rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Effectively Filed' — 35 U.S.C. 102(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: For determining whether a patent or application is prior art under 102(a)(2), the patent/application is considered effectively filed as of its actual filing date unless it is entitled to claim priority/benefit of an earlier application, in which case the effective date is the earliest such application that describes the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effectively filed date can be the actual filing date or an earlier priority date under sections 119/365/120/121/ etc., but the prior application must describe the relied‑upon subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Filing Date Rule (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'effective filing date' for a claimed invention in a patent or application is the earlier of the actual filing date of that patent/application or the filing date of the earliest priority application describing the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional, non‑provisional, international, or foreign applications can set the effective filing date for purposes of 102(a)(2) if properly claimed and supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions to Rely on an Earlier 'Effectively Filed' Date
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on an effectively filed date earlier than the actual filing date of a potential 102(a)(2) reference: (1) the U.S. patent document must claim priority to or benefit of the prior foreign/domestic application; AND (2) the prior application must describe the subject matter being relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both priority/benefit claim and sufficient written description in the earlier application are required. This difference from pre‑AIA 102(e) is significant when using foreign priority dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA FITF Exceptions — 102(b)(2)(A) and (B) for Applications/Patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure appearing in applications and patents shall not be prior art under 102(a)(2) if (A) the subject matter was obtained directly/indirectly from the inventor, or (B) the subject matter had been publicly disclosed by the inventor (or derived from the inventor) before it was effectively filed under 102(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions parallel the 102(b)(1) grace for disclosures in patent documents; provenance and timing of disclosures are critical to apply these exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA FITF Exception — Common Ownership / 102(b)(2)(C)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure appearing in applications and patents shall not be prior art under 102(a)(2) if the subject matter disclosed and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common ownership/assignment can negate certain patent‑document prior art; ownership/assignment records and timing determine applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common Ownership Under Joint Research Agreements — 35 U.S.C. §102(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter disclosed and a claimed invention are deemed owned by the same person under subsection (b)(2)(C) if: (1) both were developed by parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the claimed invention's effective filing date; (2) the claimed invention resulted from activities within the scope of the agreement; and (3) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties' names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint research agreement requirements are strict—ensure the agreement existed and scope/timing align and that parties are disclosed in the application to invoke this exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional Novelty Considerations — Analogous Art Not Required for 102
rubrics_metrics.description: For 35 U.S.C. §102 rejections, prior art need not be analogous art to the claimed invention; if a reference discloses the claimed invention, it anticipates even if the reference disparages it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP 2131.05 indicates that a reference that discloses all claim elements anticipates regardless of field or disparagement. Also, a reference that makes an element optional can anticipate a claim that expressly excludes that element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference Date Requirements to Support Art Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: To be used in a rejection under 35 U.S.C. §102 or §103, the date of a reference must qualify under 35 U.S.C. §102: for §102(a)(1) the publication date must precede applicant's effective filing date; for §102(a)(2) the effectively filed date must precede applicant's effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing the correct prior art date (publication vs effectively filed) is fundamental to whether a reference can be relied upon; mismatched dates defeat rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. §103 — Obviousness Statutory Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention may not be patented if differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date to a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manner in which the invention was made does not negate patentability. Obviousness is judged from the perspective of PHOSITA at the relevant time (pre‑AIA: time of invention; AIA: time of filing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima Facie Obviousness — Concept and PHOSITA
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness is what could readily be deduced from publicly available material or U.S. patent documents by a PHOSITA; to reject, examiner asks whether it would have been obvious to modify/combine references to arrive at the claimed invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example scenario: primary reference teaches A,B,C; second reference teaches D. Examiner must show it would have been obvious to modify the primary reference to add D to yield A,B,C,D claimed combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional Obviousness Considerations — Whole Claim and Every Element
rubrics_metrics.description: To show obviousness, each and every element of the claim must be addressed and the rejection must consider the claimed invention as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial treatment of claim elements is insufficient. Examiner must explain how the combination of references addresses all limitations and why PHOSITA would combine them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous Art Requirement for Obviousness (MPEP 2141.01(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference relied upon under §103 must be analogous prior art: (1) from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem); or (2) reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if from a different field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reference is neither in the same field nor reasonably pertinent, it should not be used to support an obviousness rejection. The examiner must justify analogy/pertinence.

rubrics_metrics.name: How Prior Art is Used for Obviousness — Teaching/Suggestion and PHOSITA Combination
rubrics_metrics.description: To show obviousness, combined prior art references or a modified single reference must teach or suggest all claim limitations and it would have been obvious to a PHOSITA to combine or modify the art accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The question is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious to PHOSITA at the relevant time. Rejections must show both the teachings and the rationale for combination/modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham v. John Deere — Four Factual Inquiries for Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: To form a basis for an obviousness rejection, make four inquiries: (1) determine the scope and contents of the prior art; (2) determine the differences between the prior art and the claims; (3) determine the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; (4) evaluate evidence of secondary considerations (commercial success, long‑felt but unsolved needs, failure of others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These Graham factors guide the legal analysis; secondary considerations can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness and must be considered when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements Required in a §103 Rejection Using Secondary Reference(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: A §103 rejection using secondary references must include: (1) description of what the primary reference teaches relative to the claimed invention; (2) identification of differences between the claimed invention and the primary reference; (3) indication of what the secondary reference(s) teach relative to those differences; (4) explanation of how the primary reference is to be modified by each secondary reference to arrive at the claimed invention and the rationale for making each modification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner must explain why each modification or combination of prior art teachings would have been obvious to PHOSITA to support the legal conclusion—mere conclusory statements are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusion — Examiner's Initial Burden
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner bears the initial burden of establishing a prima facie case of unpatentability based on either anticipation (§102) or obviousness (§103).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art rejections are essential to patent examination; applicants should understand the types of references and the legal bases of rejections to craft effective responses.
